removed.chapter: 10. Adam, Noah, and the Origin of the Law
removed.removed_text: We say: the reason for the law's necessary existence is not what the author of al-Nusrah supposed when he said it lay in the neglect of limits, their disruption, and creation's following of opposites. That is not what makes a law obligatory, nor what establishes one. We answer, rather, in our own terms. The true reason for the law's necessary existence — that is, the body of ordinances governing deeds — we have set out in our book known as al-Masabih fi al-Imamah, the Lamps in the Imamate. The most immediate ground is the need of human beings, first of all and according to their several ranks, in their very survival, for what guards them against destruction: the ordinances by which blood is preserved, by which their households, their offspring, and their wealth are fortified, and by which they are made whole in the necessary matters that arise among them. Without such ordinances, their affairs would halt and they would destroy one another. Since it is impossible, in the wisdom of the Maker Almighty, that He should deny His creatures what keeps them safe from ruin, the ordinances that are the law are of necessity present.
